newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Heartbreak looms for hard-pressed Swiss hotels.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Heartbreak looms for hard-pressed Swiss hotels.

text.p: The Swiss Hotel Museum offers a glimpse of the good old days. In 1872 the Kurhaus Bellevue, high in the Alpine village of Andermatt, advertised "air, milk or whey" cures.
Guests could avail themselves of a ladies' salon, a smoking salon, billiard and conversation rooms and dining facilities for 200. Local sights were lit up in multicoloured lights.
The hotel has gone and, with it, a lifestyle.

Today Swiss hotels, renowned for service the world over, are suffering. Overnight stays in September were at their lowest levels in 31 years, says Thomas Luethi, statistician at the Swiss Federal Statistics Office.
Alongside a cold summer and weak European economies, cheap airfares have tempted many tourists to warmer, exotic climes.
The reports are so depressing that the Swiss Tourism Assocation has recommended that the Federal Office no longer publish the "monthly horror reports."
More than half the drop has been due to fewer stays by foreign tourists, partly a result of the strong Swiss franc and the eye-popping prices it produces.
"Tourism is part of the export industry," said Rolf Bruennemann, managing director of three exclusive Buergenstock hotels perched some 700 metres (2,300 feet) above Lake Lucerne.
The Buergenstock once was a haunt for a glittering clientele including Sophia Loren, Audrey Hepburn, Henry Kissinger and Golda Meir, and the fictional James Bond in "Goldfinger."
Now the venerable complex is deep in debt. The former owner has commissioned Sotheby's to auction art from its collection.
"The Alp region is simply not in favour in the tourist industry right now," Bruenemann said.
REMNANTS OF A BYGONE AGE

According to Beat Kleiner-Frick, who with his wife runs the Hotel Museum in Zurich, luxury hotels like those in Buergenstock are remnants of an age which began around the time of Edward Whymper's ascent of the Matterhorn in 1865.
Queen Victoria spent a holiday to Lucerne in 1868 under an assumed name, the Countess of Kent.
"That was the birth of tourism in Lucerne," said Martin Nussbaumer, head of sales at the Lucerne tourist office.
Press and public were implored to leave her in peace.
Switzerland used to be a great place to go for those needing rest, peace and quiet, but times have changed.

Last winter Britain's Prince William, son of Prince Charles and Princess Diana, hid behind bodyguards at Klosters as about 30 photographers and half a dozen television crews tried to get shots of the royals during their traditonal skiing holiday in eastern Switzerland.
This year, according to British press reports, William has decided to give Klosters a miss.
Hotels are inevitably becoming more high-security.
"If someone like Prince Charles is here, he has bodyguards and the Swiss police. Other people we try to protect ourselves," said a Klosters hotel worker.
Swiss hotels also used to be nice places to die.
Empress Elizabeth of Austria, nicknamed "Sissi," was stabbed by a maniac and expired in two rooms of the Beau-Rivage in Geneva in 1898.

Today the German press is still speculating what caused the death of politician Uwe Barschel in 1987. His body was found in a bath at the same Beau Rivage. The coroner found five drugs in the corpse, discovered by two German journalists.
"We don't talk about it any more. It was such a bad experience for the image of the hotel," said one hotel official.
On the other hand, some guests seem to overstay their welcome.

Zaire's long-reigning president Mobutu Sese Seko recently left after a controversial three-month stay in a Lausanne luxury hotel, where he and his entourage of more than 20 were quartered as he recuperated from prostate surgery. The government has refused his request to return from France for a check-up.
CHANGES IN BEHAVIOUR
Gentlemen visiting Switzerland used to pursue refined activities such as curling, bobsledding, and billiards. Gentlewomen were carried up snowy peaks in sedan chairs.

An unnamed American guest has just ripped apart a lift at the five-star Beau-Rivage Palace in Lausanne (no connection with the Beau-Rivage in Geneva), causing several thousand dollars worth of damage and leaving general manager Christian Marich shaking his head.
"The biggest question for the future is the guests' behaviour," said Marich, who remains hopeful that his blend of old and new will be the ticket to the future.
The owners spent 32 million Swiss francs ($25 million) to renovate the 84-year-old hotel but kept its stained glass windows and Italian marble floors.
Marich calls up data on guests with a touch of a computer key. The guy who tore up the elevator is blacklisted. Business is profitable. The staff numbers 300 for only 180 rooms.

Marich says the key to success is his staff, but says it is a problem to find the right people in a place where the standard of living is as high as in Switzerland: "The problem is, the people. You have to get people who enjoy serving."
